  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Threat: Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
  Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Vignette:
Henry, a 61-year-old bus driver, had always prided himself on his ability to navigate the bustling streets of his city, guiding passengers safely through their daily routines. Yet, day after day, as he drove through familiar neighborhoods, there was a growing sense of dread that accompanied him. It wasn’t the traffic or the unpredictable weather that weighed heavily on him; it was the haunting memories of a traumatic experience that had left an indelible mark on his psyche.

Years ago, while on a trip abroad, Henry was captured during a violent uprising. He had been in the wrong place at the wrong time, and what followed was a harrowing ordeal of torture that stripped him of his sense of safety and self-worth. In the months that followed his release, he returned home to his wife, Linda, but the man she had known was gone. The memories of that time—filled with pain and helplessness—were like shadows that loomed over him, refusing to fade.

Now, Henry found that the nights were particularly unbearable. He would lie awake, staring at the ceiling, convinced that every creak of the house meant an intruder was entering. It had become harder for him to feel safe in his own home, a place that should have been his sanctuary. Even the smallest sounds jolted him, causing his heart to race and his body to tense. He had developed an acute vigilance, listening intently for anything that might indicate danger. Nighttime was no longer a time for rest; it was a battleground of anxiety where he fought against the ghosts of his past.

At work, his colleagues had begun to notice something was off. Henry was once a jovial presence on the bus, chatting with passengers and sharing stories. Now, he was quieter, lost in thought, often staring blankly at the road ahead. He found it difficult to concentrate, his mind drifting back to the chaos of that fateful day. Some memories were painfully vivid—the sounds of screaming, the feeling of being restrained—but other parts were frustratingly elusive, leaving him with an incomplete picture of what had transpired. He recalled the moments of sheer terror with chilling clarity, yet he struggled to remember how he escaped or what he had done to protect himself.

Each time Henry tried to recall the events, he was engulfed by the same wave of terror he had felt back then. He often found himself grappling with feelings of guilt, believing he had failed not only himself but others who were caught in the turmoil. The belief that he was weak loomed large in his mind; he would chastise himself for his inability to fight back or to help those around him. “I should have done more,” he would whisper to himself, the weight of inaction hanging over him like a dark cloud. It was a burden he carried alone, feeling unworthy of the love and support Linda offered him.

As the months turned into years, Henry’s coping mechanisms evolved into avoidance strategies. He started to withdraw from family gatherings, afraid that laughter and joy would only serve to remind him of what he had lost. Driving the bus, once a source of pride, became another reminder of the chaos of his past. He avoided certain routes that took him near places that sparked memories, opting instead for longer, safer paths that kept him away from potential triggers. Each decision to avoid left him feeling isolated, trapped in a cycle of fear that he couldn’t break.

It was only after a particularly restless night, filled with memories that felt like they were suffocating him, that Henry finally decided to seek help. He had lain awake, watching the shadows dance on the walls, and realized that he could no longer bear the burden of his memories alone. He feared the stigma of speaking about his trauma, worried that others might see him as weak or broken, but he also felt a flicker of hope. Perhaps, through therapy, he could find a way to reclaim his life, to understand the pieces of his past that had shattered him and learn to feel safe again.

As he sat in the waiting room of the clinic, heart racing and palms sweaty, Henry took a deep breath. He was terrified of what the journey ahead might entail, yet he was equally desperate for relief. What frightened him most was the thought that he might never find peace, but deep down, he was hoping for a chance to piece together the fragments of his life and learn how to navigate the world without fear.
